thread.title: Media: Why the 'Tech Problem' Is a 'Horror Story'

title: Media: Why the 'Tech Problem' Is a 'Horror Story'
text:
Large Photo: Bloomberg News 
Can the media industry do what it takes to fight back against aggressive, free-spending competitors like Amazon.com and Netflix ? 
BTIG Managing Director Rich Greenfield , who follows the media industry, published a Thursday post—titled “ Hollywood Horror Story: Invasion of the Tech Giants ”—that offered reasons why he thinks media companies might not, spurred in part by the news that Barron’s Next 50 component Netflix (NFLX) snagged producer Ryan Murphy from 21st Century Fox . 
Greenfield let us republish a lightly edited excerpt from his post: 
The challenge facing the legacy media companies who own film and television studios is that they do not own their greatest assets, meaning the talent itself. They own libraries, which clearly have and will continue to have significant value. The value of those libraries, along with new production capabilities, led many to believe that the tech giants would buy legacy media companies (remember the Apple (AAPL) for Disney (DIS) days). 
Yet, we sense the tech platforms have all realized that you do not need to spend up to buy studios, when all you need to be a major player in Hollywood is money (a lot of money) to acquire talent and produce content yourself. And maybe even more importantly to the tech platforms, creating your own content gives you complete flexibility to build and distribute the content versus the legacy entanglements created by output and licensing agreements existing studios have made. 
The irony of the current legacy media consolidation wave is that they are trying to bulk up on content ... to gain the necessary scale so they can begin to launch direct-to-consumer streaming offerings. Yet, the content is literally walking out the door to go work for the tech platforms utilizing their balance sheet strength and consumer data/relationships (critical for marketing). 
The legacy media industry remains largely incapable of entering the tech world, especially mobile. TV Everywhere has been a consumer fail to-date, with no meaningful direct-to-consumer businesses outside of premium networks such as HBO and Showtime. Even Hulu, which is likely their greatest legacy media tech success to-date, is a fraction of Netflix’s size with ballooning losses as it expands from SVOD to linear TV and is still only a domestic business. 
We continue to believe the legacy media industry’s “tech problem” is a direct result of their management compensation structure. ... We believe tying management compensation to current-year financial performance makes it nearly impossible for legacy media companies to innovate and invest aggressively enough to transition themselves away from the legacy multichannel bundle toward a direct-to-consumer streaming future. 
Barron’s , meanwhile, reported on one analyst’s take on NetFlix yesterday, noting projections of an addressable market of 700 million global subscribers by 2020 .
